newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: S.AMERICA VEGOIL SALES SAID SLOW AS GULF KICKS IN.
newsitem.headline: S.AMERICA VEGOIL SALES SAID SLOW AS GULF KICKS IN.

text.p: South American soybean oil and sunflower oil sales are slowing, but Chinese interest is keeping the last embers of the southern season alight as U.S. supply becomes competitive, Argentine traders said Wednesday.
Argentine-Dutch trader Nidera has been actively seeking oil in the Gulf, reflecting the switch from the southern to the northern oil season, a trader said.
"Nidera bought 9,000 tonnes of Gulf soyoil from ADM at about $200 over, for August shipment," he said, adding the oil was destined for Bangladesh.
But, while the South American crush rate is due to slip drastically after September, deliveries remain brisk.

"The shipping lineups are still pretty decent. We have been shipping from South America, Argentina and Brazil combined, about half a million tonnes of soyoil and sunoil a month," the trader said, "That's going to slow down, and I expect something closer to 420,000 tonnes for August, and a little slower in September."

He reported persistant Chinese interest, and intermittent buying by Iran. There are also ample freight bookings for Chile and Peru, apparently due to tight fish oil supplies caused by the El Nino current hitting west coast South American catches.
But South America is already uncompetitive in the Mediterranean, which is supplied by European rape.
Other traders reported slow oil business.
"I haven't seen much interest around here for oils," one said, "Basically China is more interested in oil from the Gulf."
Argentine soymeal exports sales were also slow, he said.
"There's been a bit going on with Denmark, some for China. But not so much going on," he said.
He added that business might pick up now that Wednesday's eagerly awaited USDA crop figures were announced.
Most interest has been for meal for September shipment, offered at about $20 under Chicago Board of Trade meal, he said.

The first trader said he had revised an earlier estimate of a one-million-tonne Sept 30 carryover of Argentine soybean meal and pellets, due to a lower-than expected June crush and a pick up in meal demand.
"I reduced the estimate to 700,000 tonnes, but it's still a record," he said.
